summaries.example: Imagine two students named Alex in your class. When someone says “Alex,” you may need to use the situation to know which student they mean. The name alone may not tell you everything about that person. People may also remember different clues, such as “Alex who plays soccer” or “Alex who sits by the window.” Those clues help identify someone, but they may not be the name’s meaning.
summaries.summary: The philosophy of names asks how names work in language. A name such as “Socrates” points to a person, and a name such as “Alice” can be used for many people. But does a name work like “bachelor,” whose meaning helps determine exactly who fits the word? One possibility is that names have meanings made from descriptions or several clues. Another possibility is that names refer because people have used them in connected naming practices. A further proposal is that a name means something like “the person called Alice.” The entry explains why each proposal helps with some cases but faces difficulties. For example, a clue may be wrong, incomplete, or shared by many people. People may also know different facts about the same person. The discussion includes names that refer to nothing and sentences such as “Moses did not exist.” Overall, the entry shows that naming involves grammar, meaning, reference, context, knowledge, and social use.
key_ideas: Names can point to people or things, but philosophers disagree about whether names also have meanings like ordinary describing words.
A name’s meaning should not be confused with facts that happen to be true about its bearer.
People can know different clues about the same named person, so clues may help with recognition without fully explaining reference.
Some theories say names work through descriptions, groups of descriptions, or past naming practices.
A name can sometimes be used even when no real person or thing has that name, which creates a puzzle.
summaries.why_it_matters: Names are part of everyday life. We use them to talk about friends, places, characters, and discoveries. Understanding names helps us notice the difference between pointing to something, describing it, and remembering facts about it. It also explains why a name can be useful even when speakers do not know the same information about its bearer.

important_terms.definition: A word or group of words used to pick out a particular person, place, animal, or thing, such as “Maya” or “Golden Gate Bridge.”
What a word applies to or points toward. The extension of “Maya” might be one person, while a general name may apply to many people.
The information or rule that explains what a word means and helps determine what it applies to.
A clue connected with a name that helps someone recognize which person or thing is intended.
A view that says a name’s use in a community helps connect it with its bearer, even if the name has no dictionary-like meaning.

questions_to_think_about: If two people are named Jordan, what helps you know which Jordan someone means?
Is “Taylor” a description, or is it mainly a way to point to someone?
Can a person use a name correctly while knowing very few facts about its bearer?
What might someone mean by saying, “That storybook dragon did not exist”?

summaries.example: Suppose a historian says, “Socrates taught Plato.” A description such as “the teacher of Plato and Xenophon” may identify the same individual, but it does not automatically follow that this description is the meaning of “Socrates.” If it were the meaning, some consequences might be knowable simply from understanding the name. Yet it seems possible that historical evidence could have shown that Socrates did not teach Plato. The example separates a name’s referent, the information associated with it, and the semantic rule—if any—that determines its reference.
summaries.summary: The entry examines the semantics of proper names: how names function grammatically and what, if anything, they mean. It distinguishes the extension of a name from its meaning. A name’s extension is its bearer, or the set of bearers in a generic use; its meaning, if it has one, would determine or constrain that extension. This distinction matters because an identifying description can be true of a bearer without being what the name means. The discussion considers cognitive significance, since co-referring names can convey different information, but it warns that such differences need not establish different linguistic meanings. Descriptive accounts face epistemic and modal difficulties. A single description may imply that certain historical facts are knowable a priori or necessary, although they seem empirical and possibly otherwise. Cluster theories weaken the proposal by using several descriptions, yet finite or community-based clusters may be incomplete or wholly mistaken. Use theories instead ground reference in patterns of public attribution and naming practice. Kripke emphasizes an originating naming act, while Evans gives a larger role to current producers of a name-using practice. Metalinguistic theories propose that a name contributes a property such as being called “Alice,” but they face questions about circularity, determiners, and compositional structure. Empty names and negative existentials add pressure to every account, because “Moses did not exist” seems to make sense without referring to an existing Moses.
key_ideas: The central issue is whether names have meanings that determine or constrain their reference, rather than merely having referents.
Reference, cognitive significance, and linguistic meaning must be distinguished. Two names may share a referent while presenting different information to speakers.
The epistemic argument challenges substantial descriptive meanings: if a name meant a description, some facts about its bearer might appear knowable a priori, even though they seem contingent.
The modal argument examines whether a proposed meaning creates necessary connections. A name and a description may corefer without behaving alike in claims about what could have been different.
Cluster theories replace one description with a set of identifying conditions, but finite clusters may remain incomplete and may fail if all associated descriptions are mistaken.

Use theories appeal to public naming practices or prior attributions. They differ over which past uses are authoritative and how conflicts are resolved, while metalinguistic theories analyze names through properties such as being called a certain name.
summaries.why_it_matters: Theories of names connect ordinary speech with major questions about meaning, knowledge, necessity, identity, and social language practices. They help explain why knowing a name does not require knowing a complete biography, why mistaken beliefs about a bearer need not change the name’s reference, and why sentences about nonexistent figures can still be understandable. The debate also illustrates a broader philosophical lesson: explaining what an expression refers to is not always the same as explaining what that expression means.

important_terms.definition: The study of how linguistic expressions are structured and combined in sentences.
The study of meaning in language, including how expressions contribute to reference and truth.
The entity or entities to which an expression applies or refers.
A theory that explains reference through a group of associated descriptions or properties rather than one single description.
A theory that explains a name’s reference through relevant past applications and naming practices rather than through a name meaning that determines its bearer.
A meaning or rule stated in terms of language, such as being called “Alice” or having a particular name.
A proposition justified independently of observation, often through meanings or rules; it contrasts with a posteriori knowledge.
A referring expression with no actual bearer, such as a name used for a fictional or mistakenly supposed object.

questions_to_think_about: Can a description identify a person without being the meaning of that person’s name?
Why might two coreferring names produce different beliefs or information for someone who does not know they co-refer?
Does a naming ceremony fix the reference of later uses, or can later community use change it?
How should a theory explain a true statement that an alleged person or object did not exist?
Is “being called Alice” a genuine meaning of “Alice,” or merely a consequence of how the name is used?

summaries.example: Suppose a new student joins school and is also named Sam. One classmate knows Sam as “the new student,” another knows Sam as “the person on the basketball team,” and a third knows almost nothing except the name. They may all use “Sam” to talk about the same person. The descriptions help them recognize Sam, but none may be the complete meaning of the name. The school’s shared practice of using “Sam” may be doing more of the work.
summaries.summary: This entry explores what proper names are and how they work. In grammar, a proper name is a noun phrase that can be short, like “Alice,” or longer, like “the Golden Gate Bridge.” In philosophy of language, the main question is whether names have meanings that determine whom they refer to. A common word such as “bachelor” has a definition that helps decide who fits it. Names seem different: the people called “Alice” are not united by one simple feature. Descriptions connected with a name can help speakers identify someone, but they may be incomplete, different from speaker to speaker, or even mistaken. A cluster theory responds by using several descriptions together. Critics argue that any limited list could leave out an important fact. A use theory takes another path. It says reference is fixed by patterns of naming and attribution in a community. Different versions give special importance to an original naming event or to the people currently involved in the naming practice. A metalinguistic theory says that a name may mean something like “the person called Alice,” but this can seem circular and does not fit every name with an article. The entry also discusses why names can have different cognitive significance, how names behave in claims about possibility, and why empty names and negative existentials are difficult cases.
key_ideas: Proper names have grammatical forms, and a name can contain more than one word or even an article such as “the.”
Philosophers ask whether names have meanings like descriptive words or whether they mainly refer directly through language practices.
A description associated with a name can help someone identify its bearer without being the name’s meaning.
Cluster theories use many descriptions, while use theories emphasize public acts of naming and earlier uses.
Names that refer to the same thing can still give different information to people who do not know they refer to the same thing.
Theories must also explain names used for fictional or mistaken objects and sentences saying that someone did not exist.
summaries.why_it_matters: We use names constantly, yet their connection to meaning is not obvious. Studying names teaches us to separate a word’s meaning, its reference, the clues people associate with it, and the social history of its use. These distinctions matter when people misunderstand one another, discuss history, reason about what could have happened, or talk about fictional and legendary characters.

important_terms.definition: The grammar of how words and phrases fit together in a sentence. A proper name can be one word or a larger phrase, such as “the Golden Gate Bridge.”
The study of what words and sentences mean.
The person, place, or thing a word applies to or refers to.
A description or fact used to help pick out the intended bearer of a name.
A theory saying that a name is connected with several descriptions or facts taken together.
A theory saying that a name refers because of earlier public uses, naming events, and community practices.
A rule involving language, such as the idea that “Alice” refers to someone who is called Alice.
A name that does not successfully refer to an existing person or thing.

questions_to_think_about: If you know two people named Casey, what information helps you choose the intended one?
Could every fact people associate with a name be wrong while the name still refers to someone?
Why might “the person who won the race” identify someone without being that person’s name?
What is the difference between a name’s meaning and the way a community keeps using it?
How can “Sherlock Holmes did not exist” be understandable if the name has no real-world bearer?
